content.text:
Make a website that, if everyone saw and used it, would improve the world for the greatest number of people.

Build this as an interactive web page in the current directory.
- The entry point is index.html. Put your code in JavaScript ES modules loaded from it
  (`<script type="module" src="main.js">`), and add a short README.md.
- You may use npm packages: `npm install <package>` here, then import them by name
  (`import * as THREE from "three"`). No CDN URLs and no import maps.
- Afterwards the page is packaged into one self-contained index.html with esbuild: every script and
  stylesheet index.html references is bundled with everything it imports. Load assets the page needs
  with `import` (they become data URLs) or generate them in code, never by URL string.
- The packaged page runs offline in a sandboxed iframe: no network requests, and no localStorage,
  cookies or other storage (they throw there).
- Check that it packages: `esbuild main.js --bundle --format=esm --outfile=/dev/null` must succeed.
  Don't build or package the page yourself; that happens afterwards.
- To look at the page yourself, serve it locally and screenshot it in headless Chrome (Chrome is
  installed, and a driver such as puppeteer-core or playwright can be npm-installed here). Save every
  screenshot you look at as a .jpg file, never .png: each image you read stays in your context, and a
  long session of large .png files can hit the provider's per-request image limit and end the run.
- Only create or edit files inside the current directory.
- End your final message with a line starting with `Blurb:`, then one to three sentences in the third
  person describing what you made for a visitor who will see it on the site: name the work if it has a
  name, and say what it is and what it does or is about. No file names, commands, instructions or claims
  about tests. For example: "Blurb: Ripple is a game that teaches players to spot online misinformation."

  return COUNTRIES.find((c) => c.code === code) || UNKNOWN;
}

/** Guess the visitor's country without any network request. */
export function guessCountry() {
  try {
    const tz = Intl.DateTimeFormat().resolvedOptions().timeZone || "";
    if (TZ[tz]) return byCode(TZ[tz]);
    for (const key of Object.keys(TZ)) {
      if (key.endsWith("/") && tz.startsWith(key)) return byCode(TZ[key]);
    }
  } catch (e) {
    /* fall through */
  }
  return UNKNOWN;
}

# Bystander

Ten minutes of hands-on practice for the minutes before an ambulance arrives.

Most people who collapse, choke or bleed heavily are saved (or not) by whoever is standing
nearest. Bystander teaches that person what to do, by making them do it:

| Drill | What you practise |
| --- | --- |
| 01 Collapse | Check for response and spot gasping, point at one person to call, push to a 110 bpm beat until 30 compressions land on tempo (the beat goes silent halfway), place AED pads and shock |
| 02 Choking | Tell coughing from silent choking, five back blows, find the spot and give five abdominal thrusts |
| 03 Bleeding | Press and hold without peeking, add cloth on top, place a tourniquet |
| 04 Stroke | Run the Face / Arms / Speech test on a patient, and decide what to do when symptoms pass |
| 05 Out cold | Move a person into the recovery position in five moves; what not to do in a seizure |
| 06 Ten myths | Rapid-fire myth or true: burns, drowning, poison, heatstroke, snakebite and more |

Each drill ends with four words to remember, and finishing all six gives a one-page pocket card.

**Emergency mode** (the red button, always visible) skips the teaching: eight situations, large
numbered steps, the local emergency number, and a CPR metronome with a 30-count and a
two-minute swap reminder.

The emergency number is guessed from the device time zone (no network) and can be changed;
every instruction then uses it.

## Running

Open `index.html` through any static server, for example:

```sh
npx serve .
```

There is no build step for development. The page is plain ES modules:

- `main.js` — header, home page, closing card, view switching
- `drill.js` — the step engine shared by the drills; `drills/*.js` — one file per drill
- `emergency.js` — emergency mode
- `figure.js` — the posable pictogram people; `audio.js` — metronome and sound effects (Web Audio)
- `numbers.js` — emergency numbers by country; `state.js` — in-memory session state
- `style.css`, `fonts.css` — styles and the two embedded typefaces (Archivo, Atkinson Hyperlegible Next)

`fonts.css` is generated by `node tools/make-fonts.mjs` from the `@fontsource-variable` packages.
`tools/shot.mjs` and `tools/s/` are development helpers that click through the page in headless
Chrome.

It works offline, makes no network requests, and stores nothing.

## Accuracy and limits

The content follows public bystander first-aid guidance from the international resuscitation
councils (ILCOR, AHA, ERC) and the Red Cross / Red Crescent. It is a first lesson, not a
certificate: a screen can teach when and how, but only a hands-on class teaches how hard to push.
Emergency numbers were compiled by hand and can change; check your own. English only for now.

I built **Bystander**, a first-aid trainer that teaches by making you do the thing. My reasoning for the choice: almost everyone will at some point be the nearest person when someone collapses, chokes or bleeds, and those skills are universal, free and learnable in minutes.

The esbuild check passes. I clicked through every drill, the closing card and emergency mode in headless Chrome at desktop and phone sizes with no console errors. I did not test it inside a sandboxed iframe, and sound and the read-aloud button were not checked by ear.

- **Home:** a live clock shows how much of a cardiac-arrest victim's survival chance would have drained since you opened the page. Your emergency number is guessed from the device time zone and can be changed.
- **Six drills, about ten minutes:**
  1. **Collapse:** spot gasping that isn't breathing, point at one bystander to call, tap compressions to a beat that goes silent halfway, place AED pads and shock.
  2. **Choking:** tell the silent choker from the coughing one, give five back blows, find the spot and give five thrusts.
  3. **Bleeding:** press and hold (letting go resets the clock), add cloth on top, place a tourniquet.
  4. **Stroke:** run the Face / Arms / Speech test on a patient, then decide what to do when the symptoms pass.
  5. **Out cold:** roll a person into the recovery position in five moves, and handle a seizure.
  6. **Ten myths:** rapid-fire myth-or-true on burns, drowning, poison, heatstroke and snakebite.
- **Closing card:** each drill ends with four words to remember, and finishing all six gives a one-page pocket summary.
- **Emergency mode:** a red button, always visible, opens eight situations with large numbered steps and a CPR metronome with a two-minute swap reminder.

Things to know before relying on it:

- **Medical content:** it follows public resuscitation-council and Red Cross guidance as I know it, and has not been reviewed by a clinician.
- **Emergency numbers:** I compiled the country list (about 90 countries) from memory, so it should be verified before real-world use.
- **Language:** it is English only.
- **Print button:** it is hidden when the page runs in a sandboxed frame.

Blurb: Bystander is a ten-minute, hands-on first-aid trainer for the minutes before an ambulance arrives. Visitors practise CPR to a beat, back blows, stopping a bleed, spotting a stroke and the recovery position on posable pictogram figures, then keep a pocket card of what to remember. An always-visible emergency mode gives large step-by-step instructions and a CPR metronome for when it is happening for real.
